The workers did not agree to the new terms offered by the trade union.

g: To yield assent to; to approve.
x: We agreed a bargain yesterday.
... and there, after a good while in discourse, we did agree a bargain of £5,000 with Sir Roger Cuttance for my Lord Sandwich for silk, cinnamon, ...
The essential idea is that parties should enter the market, choose their contractors, set their own terms and agree a bargain.

g: To make a stipulation by way of settling differences or determining a price; to exchange promises; to come to terms or to a common resolve; to promise.
x: Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison.
But he answered one of them, and said, Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny?

g: To resemble; to coincide; to correspond; to tally.
x: The picture does not agree with the original.
The two scales agree exactly.
The witnesses' stories agree in most details with the accused's.

g: To suit or be adapted in its effects; to do well.
x: The same food does not agree with every constitution.

g: To correspond to (another word) in a grammatical category, such as gender, number, case, or person.
x: In Romanian, all articles, adjectives, and pronouns agree in gender, number and case with the noun they refer to.

g: To consent to a contract or to an element of a contract.

agreement.etym: From Middle English agrement, agreement, from Old French agrement, agreement. Doublet of agrément. Morphologically agree + -ment.

g: An understanding between entities to follow a specific course of conduct.
x: to enter an agreement
The UK and US negotiators were nearing agreement.
He nodded his agreement.

g: A state whereby several parties share a view or opinion; the state of not contradicting one another.
x: The results of my experiment are in agreement with those of Michelson and with the law of General Relativity.

g: A legally binding contract enforceable in a court of law.
Rules that exist in many languages that force some parts of a sentence to be used or inflected differently depending on certain attributes of other parts.
An agreeable quality.
x: Her nymph-like features such agreements have / That I could venture with her to the grave [...].

agriculture.etym: From Middle English agriculture, partly from Middle French agriculture and partly from its etymon Latin agricultūra, from ager (“field”) + cultūra (“cultivation”). See acre and culture.

g: The art or science of cultivating the ground, including the growing and harvesting of crops, and the rearing and management of livestock.
x: Meronyms: tillage, cropping
Near-synonym: husbandry

g: An agricultural approach of using the interactive benefits from combining trees and shrubs with crops and/or livestock.
A scientist whose speciality is agronomy.

agronomy.etym: From French agronomie, from agronome (“agriculturist”), from Ancient Greek ἀγρός (agrós, “field”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). By surface analysis, agro- + -nomy.

g: The science of utilizing plants, animals and soils for food, fuel, feed, fiber, etc.
x: Near-synonym: husbandry
